claim: Prairie vole breeder pairs form monogamous pair bonds.
source: Prairie vole breeder pairs form monogamous pair bonds, which are maintained through the expression of selective aggression toward novel conspecifics.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that establishes the model system being studied.

claim: Monogamous pair bonds are maintained through the expression of selective aggression toward novel conspecifics.
source: Prairie vole breeder pairs form monogamous pair bonds, which are maintained through the expression of selective aggression toward novel conspecifics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is a well-established behavioral characteristic in the field.

claim: Pair bonding up-regulates mRNA expression for genes encoding D1-like dopamine receptors in both sexes.
source: For both sexes, we show that pair bonding up-regulates mRNA expression for genes encoding D1-like dopamine (DA) receptors and dynorphin as well as enhances stimulated DA release within the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2a,c showing increased Drd1 mRNA in paired males and females.

claim: Pair bonding up-regulates mRNA expression for genes encoding dynorphin in both sexes.
source: For both sexes, we show that pair bonding up-regulates mRNA expression for genes encoding D1-like dopamine (DA) receptors and dynorphin as well as enhances stimulated DA release within the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2a,c showing increased Pdyn mRNA in paired males and females.

claim: Pair bonding enhances stimulated DA release within the nucleus accumbens in both sexes.
source: For both sexes, we show that pair bonding up-regulates mRNA expression for genes encoding D1-like dopamine (DA) receptors and dynorphin as well as enhances stimulated DA release within the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5e,h showing increased DA release in the NAc shell of paired males and females.

claim: D1-like receptor regulation of selective aggression is mediated through downstream activation of kappa-opioid receptors.
source: We next show that D1-like receptor regulation of selective aggression is mediated through downstream activation of kappa-opioid receptors (KORs) and that activation of these receptors mediates social avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral pharmacology data in Figure 9 showing that KOR agonist administration can restore aggression when D1 receptors are blocked, but D1 agonist cannot restore aggression when KORs are blocked.

claim: Activation of kappa-opioid receptors mediates social avoidance.
source: We next show that D1-like receptor regulation of selective aggression is mediated through downstream activation of kappa-opioid receptors (KORs) and that activation of these receptors mediates social avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by partner preference data in Figure 1 showing that KOR agonist administration prior to pairing induces avoidance of the partner.

claim: Pair bonding results in sex-specific alterations in KOR binding density within the NAc shell of paired males.
source: Finally, we also identified sex-specific alterations in KOR binding density within the NAc shell of paired males and demonstrate that this alteration contributes to the neuroprotective effect of pair bonding against drug reward.
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data in Figure 3a,b showing decreased KOR binding in paired males but not females.

claim: Sex-specific alterations in KOR binding density contribute to the neuroprotective effect of pair bonding against drug reward.
source: Finally, we also identified sex-specific alterations in KOR binding density within the NAc shell of paired males and demonstrate that this alteration contributes to the neuroprotective effect of pair bonding against drug reward.
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place preference data in Figure 12 showing that KOR blockade restores amphetamine reward in paired males.

claim: Prairie voles form selective and enduring attachments to their mating partner.
source: The socially monogamous prairie vole (Michrotus ochrogaster) presents an ideal animal model to study the neural correlates of social bond maintenance because, unlike most mammals (Kleiman, 1977), prairie voles form selective and enduring attachments to their mating partner (Aragona et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The maintenance of pair bonds is associated with the expression of selective aggression towards novel conspecifics in both field and laboratory settings.
source: In both the field and laboratory, the maintenance of these bonds is associated with the expression of selective aggression towards novel conspecifics as well as selective affiliation with the mating partner (i.e., mate guarding) (Carter and Getz, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The maintenance of pair bonds is associated with selective affiliation with the mating partner (mate guarding) in both field and laboratory settings.
source: In both the field and laboratory, the maintenance of these bonds is associated with the expression of selective aggression towards novel conspecifics as well as selective affiliation with the mating partner (i.e., mate guarding) (Carter and Getz, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of selective aggression requires activation of D1-like dopamine receptors within the nucleus accumbens shell.
source: To date, laboratory studies have identified that the expression of selective aggression, and therefore pair bond maintenance, requires the activation of both D1-like dopamine (DA) and kappa-opioid receptors (KORs) within the nucleus (NAc) shell as blockade of either one of the receptors attenuates aggressive rejection of novel conspecifics (Aragona et al., 2006; Resendez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Expression of selective aggression requires activation of kappa-opioid receptors within the nucleus accumbens shell.
source: To date, laboratory studies have identified that the expression of selective aggression, and therefore pair bond maintenance, requires the activation of both D1-like dopamine (DA) and kappa-opioid receptors (KORs) within the nucleus (NAc) shell as blockade of either one of the receptors attenuates aggressive rejection of novel conspecifics (Aragona et al., 2006; Resendez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blockade of D1-like dopamine receptors within the NAc shell attenuates aggressive rejection of novel conspecifics.
source: To date, laboratory studies have identified that the expression of selective aggression, and therefore pair bond maintenance, requires the activation of both D1-like dopamine (DA) and kappa-opioid receptors (KORs) within the nucleus (NAc) shell as blockade of either one of the receptors attenuates aggressive rejection of novel conspecifics (Aragona et al., 2006; Resendez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is also confirmed by data in Figure 9.

claim: Blockade of kappa-opioid receptors within the NAc shell attenuates aggressive rejection of novel conspecifics.
source: To date, laboratory studies have identified that the expression of selective aggression, and therefore pair bond maintenance, requires the activation of both D1-like dopamine (DA) and kappa-opioid receptors (KORs) within the nucleus (NAc) shell as blockade of either one of the receptors attenuates aggressive rejection of novel conspecifics (Aragona et al., 2006; Resendez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is also confirmed by data in Figure 9.

claim: D1-like dopamine receptor and kappa-opioid receptor systems directly interact at the molecular level in other animal models.
source: Interestingly, in other animal models, these receptor systems have been shown to directly interact at the molecular level (Gerfen et al., 1990; Carlezon et al., 1998) as well as in the transition between motivational states (Chartoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: D1-like dopamine receptor and kappa-opioid receptor systems interact in the transition between motivational states in other animal models.
source: Interestingly, in other animal models, these receptor systems have been shown to directly interact at the molecular level (Gerfen et al., 1990; Carlezon et al., 1998) as well as in the transition between motivational states (Chartoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of KORs is associated with aversive states.
source: Given that activation of KORs is associated with aversive states (Mucha and Herz, 1985; Pfeiffer et al., 1986; Shippenberg and Herz, 1986; Bals-Kubik et al., 1989), we first determined if activation of NAc KORs prior to pairing with a novel social stimulus is sufficient to tag a recently encountered social stimulus as aversive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Control males treated with aCSF did not show a preference for either the partner or stranger after 1 hour cohabitation.
source: As expected, a Wilcoxon signed rank sum test for non-parametric data demonstrated that control males treated with aCSF did not show a preference for either individual (W(5) = 33, z = −0.97, p=0.33) (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: Males administered a KOR agonist into the NAc shell prior to pairing avoided the female partner and showed a preference for a novel female.
source: Conversely, male subjects that were administered a KOR agonist (1 μg U50,488) into the NAc shell immediately prior to pairing with the female partner avoided the female that had been paired with KOR activation and therefore displayed a robust preference for contact with the novel female that had not been previously paired with NAc shell KOR (Wilcoxon signed rank sum test, W(6) = 32.5, z = -2.56, p=0.01) (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: Activation of NAc shell KORs prior to pairing resulted in males spending less time in the partner's chamber and more time in the stranger's chamber.
source: In addition to differences in direct contact time, activation of NAc shell KORs prior to pairing with a social stimulus also resulted in differences in the duration of time spent in each stimulus chamber (two-way ANOVA, (F(2,36) = 7.07, p=0.003). Specifically, males that received administration of a KOR agonist avoided the chamber containing the partner (Bonferroni's post hoc test, p=0.02) and spent more time in the chamber occupied by the stranger (p=0.0006) (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Control males and males receiving KOR agonist did not differ in total contact time.
source: Finally, control males and males receiving site-specific administration of the KOR agonistdid not differ in total contact time (time spent with partner + time spent with stranger) (t-test, t(11) = 0.35, p=0.73), indicating that reduced contact with the partner did not result from a general decrease in motivation for social contact (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Control males and males administered KOR agonist did not differ in affiliative social behavior or grooming behavior during 1 hour cohabitation.
source: Both groups of male subjects also did not differ in affiliative social behavior or grooming behavior during the 1 hr cohabitation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pair bonded males showed higher levels of Pdyn mRNA within the ventral striatum compared to non-paired males.
source: Specifically, within the ventral striatum, t-test results show that pair bonded males and females showed higher levels of mRNA for the gene encoding dynorphin (Pdyn) (Male: t(24) = 2.26, p=0.03; t(26) = 3.05, p=0.005), the endogenous ligand for KORs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Pair bonded females showed higher levels of Pdyn mRNA within the ventral striatum compared to non-paired females.
source: Specifically, within the ventral striatum, t-test results show that pair bonded males and females showed higher levels of mRNA for the gene encoding dynorphin (Pdyn) (Male: t(24) = 2.26, p=0.03; t(26) = 3.05, p=0.005), the endogenous ligand for KORs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Pair bonded males showed elevated levels of Drd1 mRNA within the ventral striatum compared to non-paired males.
source: They also showed elevated levels of mRNA expression for the gene encoding D1-like receptors (Drd1) (t-test; Male: t(24) = 2.86, p=0.009; Female: t(28) = 3.42, p=0.002) (Figure 2a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Pair bonded females showed elevated levels of Drd1 mRNA within the ventral striatum compared to non-paired females.
source: They also showed elevated levels of mRNA expression for the gene encoding D1-like receptors (Drd1) (t-test; Male: t(24) = 2.86, p=0.009; Female: t(28) = 3.42, p=0.002) (Figure 2a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Differences in Drd1 and Pdyn mRNA expression were not identified within the dorsal striatum.
source: Finally, differences in the expression of mRNA for Drd1 and Pdyn were not identified within the dorsal striatum indicating that these changes are specific to the ventral region of the striatum (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical data presented in Table 2.

claim: Pair bonded males had higher levels of Drd3 mRNA within the dorsal striatum compared to non-paired males.
source: Specifically, compared to non-paired subjects, pair bonded males had higher levels of Drd3 mRNA (t-test; t(26) = 2.34, p=0.03) while pair bonded females had higher levels of Drd2 mRNA (t-test; t(26) = 2.12, p=0.04) (Figure 2b,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Pair bonded females had higher levels of Drd2 mRNA within the dorsal striatum compared to non-paired females.
source: Specifically, compared to non-paired subjects, pair bonded males had higher levels of Drd3 mRNA (t-test; t(26) = 2.34, p=0.03) while pair bonded females had higher levels of Drd2 mRNA (t-test; t(26) = 2.12, p=0.04) (Figure 2b,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Pair bonded males had lower levels of striatal KOR binding density compared to non-paired males.
source: Compared to non-paired (sibling housed) males, a two-way ANOVA indicated that pair bonded males had lower levels of striatal KOR binding density (F(1,120) = 17.51, p=0.0001; Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: The decrease in KOR binding in paired males was specific to the ventral region of the NAc shell.
source: Further examination of pair bond induced alterations in KOR binding density within the striatum of males revealed that the decrease in KOR binding was specific to the ventral region of the NAc shell (Bonferroni's post hoc test, p=0.01; Figure 3b; Table 3), the region of the striatum where KORs act to regulate selective aggression (Resendez et al., 2012) and mediate aversion (Al-Hasani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 3b and statistical analysis in Table 3.

claim: Pair bonding did not result in significant alterations in KOR binding density in females.
source: In contrast to paired males, significant alterations in KOR binding density following the establishment of a pair bond were not identified in females (F(1,108) = 3.50, p>0.06; Figure 3c,d) suggesting that pair bonding induces sex-specific alterations in KOR binding density.
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Non-paired males have significantly higher levels of KOR binding density within the striatum compared to non-paired females.
source: Prior to the establishment of a pair bond, a two-way ANOVA indicated that non-paired (sibling housed) males have significantly higher levels of KOR binding density within the striatum compared to non-paired females (two-way ANOVA, F(1,114) = 38.14, p=0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Sex differences in KOR binding density were not identified in pair bonded males and females.
source: Interestingly, these sex differences in KOR binding density were not identified in pair bonded males and females as males no longer showed higher levels in KOR binding density (two-way ANOVA, F(1,114) = 0.36, p=0.55) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The concentration of striatal DA release evoked by a single pulse stimulation significantly decreased along a dorsal to ventral gradient in males.
source: Consistent with other mammals (Jones et al., 1995; Calipari et al., 2012), the concentration of striatal DA release evoked by a single pulse stimulation ([DA]1p) significantly decreased along a dorsal to ventral gradient (one-way ANOVA; Male: F(2,30) = 17.28, p<0.000; Female: F(2,27) = 8,57, p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4c and citations to previous literature.

claim: The concentration of striatal DA release evoked by a single pulse stimulation significantly decreased along a dorsal to ventral gradient in females.
source: Consistent with other mammals (Jones et al., 1995; Calipari et al., 2012), the concentration of striatal DA release evoked by a single pulse stimulation ([DA]1p) significantly decreased along a dorsal to ventral gradient (one-way ANOVA; Male: F(2,30) = 17.28, p<0.000; Female: F(2,27) = 8,57, p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4e and citations to previous literature.

claim: The NAc core and NAc shell had significantly lower levels of stimulated DA release compared to the dorsal striatum in males.
source: Post hoc Tukey comparisons revealed that both the NAc core (Male: p=0.009; Female: p=0.04) and the NAc shell (Male: p=0.000; Female: p=0.001) had significantly lower levels of stimulated DA release compared to the dorsal striatum (Figure 4c,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The NAc core and NAc shell had significantly lower levels of stimulated DA release compared to the dorsal striatum in females.
source: Post hoc Tukey comparisons revealed that both the NAc core (Male: p=0.009; Female: p=0.04) and the NAc shell (Male: p=0.000; Female: p=0.001) had significantly lower levels of stimulated DA release compared to the dorsal striatum (Figure 4c,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The greatest ratio of evoked DA release occurred within the NAc shell in males.
source: This effect is represented by the greatest ratio of evoked DA release ([DA]20p/[DA]1p) within the NAc shell (Tukey post hoc test; Male: p=0.0002; Female: p=0.0004), an intermediate ratio within the NAc core (Tukey post hoc test; Male: p=0.02; Female: p=0.03), and the lowest ratio within the dorsal striatum (Figure 4d,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The greatest ratio of evoked DA release occurred within the NAc shell in females.
source: This effect is represented by the greatest ratio of evoked DA release ([DA]20p/[DA]1p) within the NAc shell (Tukey post hoc test; Male: p=0.0002; Female: p=0.0004), an intermediate ratio within the NAc core (Tukey post hoc test; Male: p=0.02; Female: p=0.03), and the lowest ratio within the dorsal striatum (Figure 4d,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Significant sex-differences in striatal DA release following a 20-pulse stimulation occurred within the dorsal striatum.
source: In addition, a two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni's post hoc tests identified significant sex-differences in striatal DA release following a 20-pulse stimulation within the dorsal striatum (F(1,10) = 5.25, p=0.002; p=0.03, Figure 4g) as well as the NAc core (F(1,34) = 4.05, p=0.05; p=0.05, Figure 4h), but not the NAc shell (F(1,32) = 1.77, p=0.1, Figure 4i).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Significant sex-differences in striatal DA release following a 20-pulse stimulation occurred within the NAc core.
source: In addition, a two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni's post hoc tests identified significant sex-differences in striatal DA release following a 20-pulse stimulation within the dorsal striatum (F(1,10) = 5.25, p=0.002; p=0.03, Figure 4g) as well as the NAc core (F(1,34) = 4.05, p=0.05; p=0.05, Figure 4h), but not the NAc shell (F(1,32) = 1.77, p=0.1, Figure 4i).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: No sex-differences in striatal DA release following a 20-pulse stimulation occurred within the NAc shell.
source: In addition, a two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni's post hoc tests identified significant sex-differences in striatal DA release following a 20-pulse stimulation within the dorsal striatum (F(1,10) = 5.25, p=0.002; p=0.03, Figure 4g) as well as the NAc core (F(1,34) = 4.05, p=0.05; p=0.05, Figure 4h), but not the NAc shell (F(1,32) = 1.77, p=0.1, Figure 4i).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Pair bonding significantly increased peak DA release within the NAc shell of pair bonded males.
source: As predicted, t-test comparisons indicated that pair bonding significantly increased peak DA release within the NAc shell of pair bonded voles (Male: t(17) = 2.44, p=0.03; Female: t(13) = 2.48, p=0.03), but not other regions of the striatum (Dorsal striatum male: t(21) = 0.09, p=1.75; Dorsal striatum female: t(17) = 1.26, p=0.22; NAc core male: t(18) = 0.87, p=0.40; NAc core female: t(15) = 0.73, p=0.48) (Figure 5c–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Pair bonding significantly increased peak DA release within the NAc shell of pair bonded females.
source: As predicted, t-test comparisons indicated that pair bonding significantly increased peak DA release within the NAc shell of pair bonded voles (Male: t(17) = 2.44, p=0.03; Female: t(13) = 2.48, p=0.03), but not other regions of the striatum (Dorsal striatum male: t(21) = 0.09, p=1.75; Dorsal striatum female: t(17) = 1.26, p=0.22; NAc core male: t(18) = 0.87, p=0.40; NAc core female: t(15) = 0.73, p=0.48) (Figure 5c–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: The average percent increase in NAc shell DA release was lower in males (34%) compared to females (99%).
source: Additionally, although pair bonding significantly elevated NAc shell DA release in both sexes, the average percent increase was lower in males (34%) compared to females (99%) (Figure 5e,h).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 5e,h.

claim: Pair bonded females had significantly higher levels of DA release within the NAc shell compared to pair bonded males.
source: Direct comparisons of peak DA release between pair bonded males and females indicated that pair bonded females had significantly higher levels of DA release within the NAc shell compared to that of pair bonded males (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Males from optimally pregnant pairs showed significantly higher levels of aggression than males from sub-optimally pregnant pairs.
source: Following 2 weeks of cohabitation with an opposite sex partner, males from optimally pregnant pairs showed significantly higher levels of aggression than males from sub-optimally pregnant pairs (t-test, t(9) = 2.54, p=0.03) (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Reproductive status had no impact on pair bond strength in paired females.
source: In contrast, reproductive status had no impact on pair bond strength in paired females as females from optimally and sub-optimally pregnant pairs did not differ in levels of selective aggression (t-test, t(9) = 0.24, p=0.82) (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Only males from optimally pregnant pairs showed significantly higher levels of selective aggression than females.
source: Specifically, although paired males are generally more aggressive than paired females, when aggression levels were further compared by fecundity classification, only males from optimally pregnant pairs showed significantly higher levels of selective aggression than females (Bonferroni's post hoc test, optimally pregnant: p=0.01, sub-optimally pregnant: p>0.99) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only males from optimally pregnant pairs showed significantly greater elevations in NAc shell DA release compared to non-paired males.
source: Specifically, examination of DA release properties in relation to the pairs reproductive status revealed that only males from optimally pregnant pairs showed significantly greater elevations in NAc shell DA release compared to non-paired males (one-way ANOVA, F(3,39) = 0.29, p=0.05; Dunnett's post hoc test, p=0.04) (Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Reproductive status did not influence NAc shell DA transmission dynamics of paired females.
source: In contrast to paired males, reproductive status did not influence NAc shell DA transmission dynamics of paired females (one-way ANOVA, F(3,31) = 1.67, p=0.20).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: For paired males, the magnitude of stimulated DA release was positively correlated with neonatal weight.
source: For paired males, the magnitude of stimulated DA release was positively correlated with neonatal weight, with fecundity accounting for nearly 30% of the variation (linear regression, R2 = 0.29, F(1,20) = 8.16, p=0.01) (Figure 6e).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: There was no relationship between fecundity and the magnitude of stimulated DA release within the NAc shell of paired females.
source: Conversely, there was no relationship between fecundity and the magnitude of stimulated DA release within the NAc shell DA of paired females (linear regression, R2 = 0.32, F(1,8) = 3.77, p=0.09 (Figure 6f).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: For pair bonded males, the intensity of aggression directed toward a resident intruder was positively correlated with NAc shell DA release.
source: For pair bonded males, the intensity of aggression directed toward a resident intruder was positively correlated with NAc shell DA release, accounting for over 40% of the variation (linear regression, R2 = 0.41, F(1,9) = 6.32, p=0.03) (Figure 6g).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 6g.

claim: No relationship between NAc shell DA release and selective aggression was identified in paired females.
source: In contrast, no relationship between NAc shell DA release and selective aggression was identified in paired females (linear regression, R2 = 0.32, F(1,8) = 3.77, p=0.09) (Figure 6h).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 6h.

claim: Bath application of a KOR agonist reduced stimulated DA release within the NAc shell of non-pair bonded voles.
source: Similar to other rodent species (Britt and McGehee, 2008), bath application of a KOR agonist (BRL 5237) onto striatal slices of non-pair bonded voles reduced stimulated DA release within the NAc shell (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 7a,b and citation to previous literature.

claim: The concentration response curves for KOR agonist effects on DA release did not significantly differ between non-paired males and females.
source: Similar effects on DA transmission were observed in both non-paired males and females as the concentration response curves did not significantly differ between the sexes (two-way ANOVA, F(1, 5) = 1.59, p=0.26).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Non-paired males and females did not differ in the IC50 of the KOR agonist.
source: Moreover, a t-test did not identify significant sex differences in the dose required to achieve a 50% reduction in DA release (IC50: t(5) = 0.03, p=0.98; Figure 7C) or in the slope of the concentration response curve (t(5) = 1.28, p=0.26, Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Non-paired males and females did not differ in the slope of the KOR agonist concentration response curve.
source: Moreover, a t-test did not identify significant sex differences in the dose required to achieve a 50% reduction in DA release (IC50: t(5) = 0.03, p=0.98; Figure 7C) or in the slope of the concentration response curve (t(5) = 1.28, p=0.26, Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Pair bonding resulted in a leftward shift in the KOR agonist concentration response curve in males.
source: More specifically, in male prairie voles, pair bonding resulted in a leftward shift in the concentration response curve (two-way ANOVA, F(1, 6) = 15.67, p=0.008) and significantly larger reductions in stimulated DA release at multiple concentrations of the KOR agonist (Bonferroni's post hoc test; 0.1 μM, p=0.03;. 3 μM, p=0.0007; 1 μM, p=0.0004; 3 μM, p=0.0003; 10 μM, p=0.002; 20 μM, p=0.02) (Figure 7f).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: A lower dose of the KOR agonist was needed to achieve a 50% decrease in stimulated DA release within the NAc shell of pair bonded males compared to non-paired males.
source: Comparison of the IC50 between paired and non-paired voles revealed that a lower dose of the KOR agonist was needed to achieve a 50% decrease in stimulated DA release within the NAc shell of pair bonded males (t-test; IC50; t(6) = 4.92, p=0.002, Figure 7h).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 7h.

claim: The slope of the KOR agonist concentration response curve significantly differed between paired and non-paired males.
source: The slope of the concentration response curve also significantly differed between paired and non-paired males (t-test; t(6) = 3.74, p=0.009, Figure 7i).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 7i.

claim: IC50 and slope of the KOR agonist concentration response curve did not significantly differ between paired and non-paired females.
source: Given that the density of KOR binding is reduced in pair bonded males, these data suggest that pair bonding may result in mechanistic changes in the function of the KOR in males, but not females, as similar measures did not significantly differ between paired and non-paired females (IC50: t-test; t(6) = 1.36, p=0.22; Figure 7J and slope: t-test; t(6) = 0.55, p=0.60; Figure 7k).
evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data shown in Figure 7j,k.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of NAc shell D1-like receptors significantly attenuated measures of selective aggression in pair bonded males.
source: As expected, pharmacological blockade of NAc shell D1-like receptors significantly attenuated measures of selective aggression in both pair bonded males (Attack frequency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.03, Attack latency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.04) and females (Attack frequency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral pharmacology data shown in Figure 9d,e.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of NAc shell D1-like receptors significantly attenuated attack frequency in pair bonded females.
source: As expected, pharmacological blockade of NAc shell D1-like receptors significantly attenuated measures of selective aggression in both pair bonded males (Attack frequency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.03, Attack latency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.04) and females (Attack frequency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral pharmacology data shown in Figure 9f.

claim: Activation of KORs in the presence of D1-antagonist restored selective aggression to levels of paired controls in males.
source: Activation of KORs in the presence of the D1-antagonist restored selective aggression as mean attack frequency (Male: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.92; Female: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.62) and attack latency (Male: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.54; Female: planned contrast, post hoc: p=1.00) did not differ from paired controls in either sex, suggesting that D1-like receptors mediate selective aggression through downstream activation of the dynorphin/KOR system.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral pharmacology data shown in Figure 9d,e.

claim: Activation of KORs in the presence of D1-antagonist restored selective aggression to levels of paired controls in females.
source: Activation of KORs in the presence of the D1-antagonist restored selective aggression as mean attack frequency (Male: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.92; Female: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.62) and attack latency (Male: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.54; Female: planned contrast, post hoc: p=1.00) did not differ from paired controls in either sex, suggesting that D1-like receptors mediate selective aggression through downstream activation of the dynorphin/KOR system.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral pharmacology data shown in Figure 9f,g.

claim: D1-like receptor activation in the presence of KOR inactivation was insufficient to restore measures of selective aggression to levels of paired controls in males.
source: In contrast, D1-like receptor activation in the presence of KOR inactivation was insufficient to restore measures of selective aggression to levels of paired controls (Male attack frequency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.006; Female attack frequency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.008; Male attack latency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.001; Female attack latency; planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.005; Figure 9d–g), further suggesting that KOR mediation of selective aggression is downstream of D1-like receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral pharmacology data shown in Figure 9d,e.

claim: D1-like receptor activation in the presence of KOR inactivation was insufficient to restore measures of selective aggression to levels of paired controls in females.
source: In contrast, D1-like receptor activation in the presence of KOR inactivation was insufficient to restore measures of selective aggression to levels of paired controls (Male attack frequency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.006; Female attack frequency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.008; Male attack latency: planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.001; Female attack latency; planned contrast, post hoc: p=0.005; Figure 9d–g), further suggesting that KOR mediation of selective aggression is downstream of D1-like receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral pharmacology data shown in Figure 9f,g.

claim: Male subjects exposed to a rewarding regimen of AMPH showed significantly altered patterns of striatal KOR expression.
source: Compared to control males (3 injections of saline across 3 days), male subjects exposed to a rewarding regimen of AMPH showed significantly altered patterns of striatal KOR expression (two-way ANOVA, F(1,78) = 15.97, p=0.0001, Figure 10a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 10a,b.

claim: AMPH exposure significantly reduced KOR expression within the dorso-medial NAc shell of males.
source: Moreover, the pattern of AMPH induced alterations in KOR expression within the striatum of males was similar to the pattern induced by pair bonding, with AMPH exposure significantly reducing KOR expression within the dorso-medial (Bonferroni's post hoc test, p=0.02) and ventral NAc shell (Bonferroni's post hoc test, p=0.01) (Figure 10b, Table 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 10b.

claim: AMPH exposure significantly reduced KOR expression within the ventral NAc shell of males.
source: Moreover, the pattern of AMPH induced alterations in KOR expression within the striatum of males was similar to the pattern induced by pair bonding, with AMPH exposure significantly reducing KOR expression within the dorso-medial (Bonferroni's post hoc test, p=0.02) and ventral NAc shell (Bonferroni's post hoc test, p=0.01) (Figure 10b, Table 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 10b.

claim: AMPH exposure had no significant impact on striatal KOR expression in females.
source: In contrast, AMPH exposure had no significant impact on striatal KOR expression in females (two-way ANOVA, F(1,108) = 0.44, p=0.51, Figure 10c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor autoradiography data shown in Figure 10c,d.

claim: Only males from pregnant pairs exhibited protection against AMPH reward.
source: Moreover, when these males were further classified by the pair's pregnancy status, only males from pregnant pairs exhibited protection against AMPH reward as males from both optimally (p>0.99) and sub-optimally pregnant pairs (p=0.94) did not form a preference for the AMPH paired chamber, while males from non-pregnant pairs formed significant preferences (p=0.006) (Figure 11a inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place preference data shown in Figure 11a.

claim: In males from optimally pregnant pairs, the rewarding properties of AMPH were negatively correlated with the pregnancy status of the female.
source: Specifically, in males from optimally pregnant pairs, the rewarding properties of AMPH were negatively correlated with the pregnancy status of the female (linear regression, R2= 0.403, F(1,9) = 6.079, p=0.036, Figure 11b).
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place preference data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 11b.

claim: A similar relationship between AMPH reward and pregnancy status was not found in males from sub-optimally pregnant pairs.
source: However, a similar relationship was not found in males from sub-optimally pregnant pairs (linear regression, R2= 0.025, F(1,6) = 0.155, p=0.708, Figure 11c).
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place preference data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 11c.

claim: Paired males treated with saline spent significantly less time in the AMPH paired chamber compared to non-paired males.
source: Specifically, compared to non-paired males that received saline injections prior to AMPH conditioning, paired males treated with saline spent significantly less time in the AMPH paired chamber (Bonferroni's post hoc test, p=0.004, Figure 12a).
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place preference data shown in Figure 12a.

claim: Global blockade of KORs in pair bonded males restored the rewarding properties of AMPH.
source: In contrast, global blockade of KORs in pair bonded males restored the rewarding properties of AMPH as paired males that received peripheral injections of nor-BNI prior to AMPH conditioning did not differ from non-paired males in the duration of time spent in the AMPH paired chamber (p>0.99, Figure 12a).
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place preference data shown in Figure 12a.

claim: Site-specific blockade of NAc shell KORs was sufficient to restore AMPH preference in pair bonded males.
source: Compared to non-paired males, paired males that received site-specific injections of aCSF into the NAc prior to AMPH conditioning spent significantly less time in the AMPH paired chamber (Bonferroni's post hoc test, p = 0.003, Figure 12c). However, pair bonded males that were administered nor-BNI prior to AMPH conditioning did not differ from non-paired males that also received site-specific administration of nor-BNI in the duration of time spent in the AMPH paired chamber (p>0.99, Figure 12c).
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place preference data shown in Figure 12c.

claim: KORs in the NAc shell are involved in pair bond induced neuroprotection against drug reward.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that KORs in the NAc shell are indeed involved in pair bond induced neuroprotection against drug reward as activation of these receptors is required for pair bond induced attenuation of drug reward.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the conditioned place preference data in Figure 12.

claim: The prairie vole KOR is distinct from that of guinea pigs, humans, rats, and mice.
source: Indeed, the prairie vole KOR is distinct from the above-mentioned species as its genetic sequence diverges from that of rats and mice (whose KOR structure is quite homologous) as well as humans and guinea pigs (whose KORs also share substantial homologies) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic sequence analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are fifteen amino acids that are unique to prairie voles in the KOR sequence.
source: In total, there are four amino acids that are unique to prairie voles, humans, and guinea pigs (Alanine 28, Serine 186, Aspartic acid 218, Aspartic acid 374), one amino acid that is unique to humans and prairie voles (Isoleucine 232), and fifteen amino acids that are unique to prairie voles, including one residue that is located in the dynorphin binding site (Rasakham and Liu-Chen, 2011; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic sequence analysis and citations to previous literature.

claim: One amino acid unique to prairie voles is located in the dynorphin binding site of the KOR.
source: In total, there are four amino acids that are unique to prairie voles, humans, and guinea pigs (Alanine 28, Serine 186, Aspartic acid 218, Aspartic acid 374), one amino acid that is unique to humans and prairie voles (Isoleucine 232), and fifteen amino acids that are unique to prairie voles, including one residue that is located in the dynorphin binding site (Rasakham and Liu-Chen, 2011; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic sequence analysis and citations to previous literature.

claim: Pair bonding increases D1 receptor expression within the ventral striatum.
source: We focused on KORs in the present study because it has previously been shown that pair bonding increases the expression of D1-like receptors specifically within the ventral striatum (Aragona et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and is also confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: Pair bonding exerts protective effects against AMPH reward.
source: Pair bonding exerts protective effects against AMPH reward (Liu et al., 2011); however, the establishment of a pair bond is associated with a complex suite of socially related experiences, such as exposure to a novel social stimulus, extended periods of cohabitation, the development of social familiarity, copulation, and impregnation and it is not well understood how these individual components contribute to the neural protective effects that pair bonding exerts against drug reward (Resendez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and is also confirmed by data in Figure 11 and 12.

claim: The establishment of a fully developed pair bond, and not other associated social experiences, mediates social buffering of drug reward.
source: Together, these data indicate that the establishment of a fully developed pair bond, and not the other associated social experiences, mediates social buffering of drug reward.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the conditioned place preference data in Figure 11.

claim: Both pair bonded males and females increased levels of selective aggression toward novel conspecifics following the establishment of a pair bond.
source: Prior to pair bonding, both males and females show low levels of aggression. However, following the establishment of a pair bond, both (a) males (Mann-Whitney test, U(1,22) = 33, z = −2.26, p = 0.03) (n = 11–13/group) and (b) females increased levels of selective aggression toward novel conspecifics (Mann-Whitney test, U(1, 15) = 11, z = −2.34, p = 0.03) (n = 6–11/group) with males showing qualitatively higher levels of aggression.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stimulation of D1-like receptors phosphorylates CREB to induce the expression and release of dynorphin.
source: Specifically, stimulation of D1-like receptors phosphorylates cAMP response element binding protein (CREB) to induce the expression and release of dynorphin (Carlezon et al., 1998), resulting in the valence encoding of a psychostimulant to be reversed from rewarding to aversive (Pliakas et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dynorphin is the endogenous ligand for KORs.
source: Specifically, within the ventral striatum, t-test results show that pair bonded males and females showed higher levels of mRNA for the gene encoding dynorphin (Pdyn) (Male: t(24) = 2.26, p=0.03; t(26) = 3.05, p=0.005), the endogenous ligand for KORs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: D1-like receptors are primarily of the low-affinity sub-type.
source: These receptors are primarily of the low-affinity sub-type (Richfield et al., 1989) and their activation requires high concentrations of DA to be released, such as that which occurs during burst firing of DA neurons (Gonon, 1997; Cheer et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of D1-like receptors requires high concentrations of DA to be released.
source: These receptors are primarily of the low-affinity sub-type (Richfield et al., 1989) and their activation requires high concentrations of DA to be released, such as that which occurs during burst firing of DA neurons (Gonon, 1997; Cheer et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: High concentrations of DA release occur during burst firing of DA neurons.
source: These receptors are primarily of the low-affinity sub-type (Richfield et al., 1989) and their activation requires high concentrations of DA to be released, such as that which occurs during burst firing of DA neurons (Gonon, 1997; Cheer et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pairing of a previously neutral stimulus with KOR activation results in avoidance of that stimulus during subsequent encounters.
source: For example, pairing of a previously neutral stimulus with either an aversive experience that results in KOR activation, such as stress, or with direct pharmacological activation of these receptors results in the avoidance of that stimulus during subsequent encounters (Land et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of NAc shell KORs is required for the expression of selective aggression by pair bonded voles.
source: Activation of NAc shell KORs is required for the expression of selective aggression by pair bonded voles (Resendez et al., 2012); however, the psychological processes that underlie the expression of this behavior are not well understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of KORs has been shown to induce aversion and mediate avoidance behaviors in other rodent species.
source: In other rodent species, activation of these receptors has been shown to induce aversion as well as mediate avoidance behaviors (Land et al., 2008; Al-Hasani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reduced activity has been observed within the VP following exposure to aversive stimuli.
source: Interestingly, reduced activity has been observed directly within the VP following exposure to aversive stimuli (Itoga et al., 2016) as well as an increase in activity within brain nuclei that receive input specifically from GABAergic neurons located within the lateral region of VP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Partner preferences require concurrent activation of D2-like and OT receptors within the NAc shell.
source: Indeed, studies of pair bond formation show that partner preferences require concurrent activation of D2-like and OT receptors within the NAc shell (Liu and Wang, 2003) as well as V1a receptor activation within the VP (Lim et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Partner preferences require V1a receptor activation within the VP.
source: Indeed, studies of pair bond formation show that partner preferences require concurrent activation of D2-like and OT receptors within the NAc shell (Liu and Wang, 2003) as well as V1a receptor activation within the VP (Lim et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Peptide systems are necessary for social recognition while DA transmission is important for reward processing.
source: These previous studies argued that peptide systems are necessary for social recognition, while DA transmission is important for reward processing (Young and Wang, 2004; Johnson and Young, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of NAc KORs reduces DA release within this region.
source: Activation of KORs within the NAc reduces DA release within this region (Britt and McGehee, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and is also confirmed by data in Figure 7.

claim: The dynorphin/KOR system robustly decreases dopaminergic transmission within the NAc.
source: One hypothesized mechanism in which the dynorphin/KOR is thought to negatively impact motivation and reward processing is through its ability to robustly decrease dopaminergic transmission within the NAc (Shippenberg et al., 1996; Carlezon and Thomas, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In drug-addicted humans, the presence of positive social support reduces the propensity for relapse.
source: For example, in drug-addicted humans, the presence of positive social support reduces the propensity for relapse (Creswell et al., 2015), suggesting that positive social experience, such as bonding, may wire the brain in a manner that reduces future drug seeking behavior (Young et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of NAc D1-like receptors, but not D2-like receptors, is required for pair bond induced protection against drug reward.
source: Indeed, it has previously been demonstrated that activation of neural systems that mediate pair bond maintenance (NAc D1-like receptors), but not those that mediate pair bond formation (NAc D2-like receptors), are required for pair bond induced protection against drug reward (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Drugs that act at the dynorphin/KOR system are currently under investigation as potential therapeutics for the treatment of addiction.
source: Given that drugs that act at the dynorphin/KOR system are currently under intense investigation as potential therapeutics for the treatment of addiction (Carlezon and Miczek, 2010) and that pair bonding induces neural plasticity within this system to result in an attenuation in drug reward, there may be considerable therapeutic value in understanding the neural mechanisms in which social experiences alter reward circuitry to buffer against drug reward.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: G protein-coupled receptors can adopt multiple conformational states, resulting in variability in ligand binding affinity and efficacy.
source: However, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRS), including KORs, are dynamic proteins that can adopt multiple conformational states, resulting in variability in ligand binding affinity as well as efficacy of the receptor to activate distinct downstream signaling cascades (Bruchas and Chavkin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: G proteins can pre-couple with receptors.
source: For example, G proteins have been shown to pre-couple with receptors (Nobles et al., 2005) and this coupling can lead to conformational changes in the extracellular portion of the receptor that enhance affinity of the ligand for the receptor (Yan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G protein pre-coupling with receptors can lead to conformational changes that enhance ligand affinity.
source: For example, G proteins have been shown to pre-couple with receptors (Nobles et al., 2005) and this coupling can lead to conformational changes in the extracellular portion of the receptor that enhance affinity of the ligand for the receptor (Yan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The percent of G protein receptor coupling can vary as a function of receptor density.
source: Moreover, the percent of G protein receptor coupling can vary as a function of receptor density (Yan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: KORs are found on the terminal regions of multiple inputs to the NAc including glutamatergic, GABAergic, and dopaminergic inputs.
source: Finally, given that KORs are found on the terminal regions of multiple inputs to the NAc (glutamatergic, GABAergic, and dopaminergic) (Meshul and McGinty, 2000; Svingos et al., 2001; Hjelmstad and Fields, 2003) more work will also be necessary to determine if KOR binding is globally decreased within the NAc of pair bonded males or if this decrease is restricted to a specific sub-population of inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.
